chapter_title: The Chapter of Fasting, for it engenders a Host of Angels
chapter_note: This kephalaion is dominated by hagiographic dialogue frame and institutional/pastoral material (elect/catechumens, lord’s day fasts, church leadership, building churches, alms, exemption from office). The key doctrinal claim—‘seven angels’ engendered by fasting—is presented only as a church-practice rule and is immediately embedded in congregational narrative and exhortation, not in a self-contained cosmic mapping/mechanics exposition. No recoverable pre-compilation correspondential substrate is present in a form separable from the later ecclesial setting.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic opening scene (⟨p.193⟩; ‘Once again, it happened… the apostle… among the congregation’), disciple-to-master address, and church categories (elect/catechumens, lord’s day). Even the ‘seven angels’ claim enters here as reported speech within the compiled dialogue frame.
Institutional self-report (‘became leader… elect… in the church… head’). No cosmos→cosmos mapping; fasting is treated as a church work in summary.
Practical accounting of fasts on ‘three lord’s days’ and counting angels engendered by ‘these elect’. This is administrative/narrative application within church life, not systematic cosmology.
Continues the administrative arithmetic of angel totals and personal gratitude for ‘profit and good’ achieved on lord’s days—an institutional piety register, not substrate exposition.

Anxiety about sin arising from commanding/authorizing church necessities (‘because of a church, to build… construct… ordinance of their church’). Application voice (‘I command… I shall question myself’) anchors the concern in governance and responsibility, not cosmic structure.

Direct supplication formula (‘Now I entreat you, my master… Perform this grace… release me…’) plus role-language (‘power [of] protection of the gods and angels’) within the disciple’s request scene—typical dialogue-frame rhetoric.
Narrative transition (‘Then, when the apostle had heard…’) describing the apostle’s response—editorial storytelling rather than teaching content.

Though introduced by a dialogue tag (‘The apostle says…’), the substance is admonitory reasoning about the ‘benefit’ of fasts on the lord’s day and rebuke for seeking exemption—hortatory pastoral discourse, not substrate mechanics.

Exhortation to persist in entrusted work despite illness; eschatological encouragement (‘land of rest… children of the living’) functions motivationally and remains tied to duty, not a degree-structure cosmology.
Promise/encouragement speech with second-person orientation (‘it will be told to you… I will… you wish… complete the good’). Pure application voice.
Argument from institutional necessity (‘if you can ask exemption… who will do it?’) and moral warning about sin—church-operational rationale, not ancient correspondential mapping.
Imperative reinforcement (‘do the work… do not strive to ask exemption’)—direct governance of behavior; no cosmological correspondential system presented.
Explicit institutional valuation (‘preaches, building the church’ vs. private edification). This is ecclesial programmatic material.
Addresses fear of sin in proclaiming about ‘building a church or alms’; reassures the worker ‘has no sin therein’—institutional ethics/application.
Contrasts righteous commanding for church work with speaking for ‘his own need… flesh’; assigns ‘utterly… sin’. Moral/pastoral casuistry, not substrate cosmology.
Direct commission (‘I assign to you… preach and… build the church of God’)—pure institutional charge and benefit-accounting.
Formulaic closing response: disciple ‘paid homage’, address ‘My master…’, pledge to ‘preach and build the church’, and request for aid—typical hagiographic closure.
